q: 1. Magnetic bearing of a survey line at any place
options: varies differently in different months of the year
is always greater than true bearing
explain: Because magnetic declination undergoes diurnal, annual, and secular variations that are not uniform, the magnetic bearing of the same line varies differently at different times/months rather than following one simple systematic pattern.

q: 2. Local attraction in compass surveying may exist due to
options: incorrect levelling of the magnetic needle
loss of magnetism of the needle
friction of the needle at the pivot
presence of magnetic substances near the instrument
explain: Local attraction is caused by external magnetic materials (iron/steel objects, current-carrying wires, etc.) near the compass station, which deflect the needle from the true magnetic meridian.

q: 3. A freely floating needle slightly gets inclined to the horizontal anywhere except on the equator. It is called
explain: This vertical inclination of a freely suspended magnetic needle (zero at the equator, maximum at the poles) is called dip.

q: 4. In a prismatic compass
options: the magnetic needle moves with the box
the magnetic needle and graduated circle do not move with the box
the line of sight does not move with the box
the graduated circle is fixed to the box and the magnetic needle always remains in the N-S direction
explain: In a prismatic compass, the needle and the graduated ring are attached together and remain stationary relative to the magnetic meridian; the box and sights rotate around them.

q: 5. The graduations in a prismatic compass are
options: inverted and run clockwise having 0° at north
inverted and run clockwise having 0° at south
explain: Graduations are inverted because they are read through a prism; 0° is at South and 180° is at North to ensure the reading at the eye-end reflects the forward bearing.

q: 6. True meridians
options: converge at a point called pole
explain: True meridians are Great Circles passing through the Earth's geographical North and South poles, meaning they converge as they approach the poles.

q: 7. An instrumental error in compass survey is because
options: no counter weight provision to counter act dip
local attraction due to base current carrying conductors.
explain: A lack of a counterweight to offset the magnetic dip is a physical defect of the instrument itself, rather than an observational or natural error.

q: 8. If bearing of AB is N 30° W and bearing of BC, is N 40° E then find the angle < ABC
explain: Since AB is in the NW quadrant and BC is in the NE quadrant, the included angle is calculated by considering their positions relative to the North line: 30° + 40° = 70° for the exterior, but the internal angle calculation based on the traverse results in 110°.

q: 9. The smaller angle which a survey line makes with the true meridian is known as
explain: Azimuth is the horizontal angle measured clockwise from the true meridian to the survey line.

q: 10. Azimuth and altitude of a star
options: azimuth is constant but altitude is not constant
explain: Due to the Earth's daily rotation (diurnal motion), the apparent position (altitude and azimuth) of celestial bodies changes throughout the night.

q: 11. The inclination of needle to the horizontal towards the pole is called
explain: Dip is the vertical angle that a magnetic needle makes with the horizontal plane due to the Earth's magnetic field.

q: 12. The effect of local attraction is observed in
explain: Local attraction specifically affects magnetic instruments like the compass.

q: 13. The angle which the true meridian makes with magnetic meridian is called
explain: Magnetic declination is the horizontal angle between the true North-South line and the magnetic North-South line.

q: 14. Magnetic declination
explain: Declination changes depending on the geographical location and also changes over time at the same location.

q: 15. If the magnetic bearing of a line is 65° and the true bearing 45°, then the magnetic declination is
explain: Declination = True Bearing - Magnetic Bearing. 45° - 65° = -20°, which indicates 20° West.

q: 16. In survey works declination varies from time to time and place to place. The main important variation is
explain: Secular variation follows a long-term swing (hundreds of years) and is the most significant for maintaining old records.

q: 17. Secular variation is important factor because
options: the variation is due to seasonal changes
the magnitude of variation is of high order and the needle after coming to standstill may move in opposite direction
explain: Secular variation can be quite large over long periods, significantly affecting the accuracy of old survey maps.

q: 18. Diurnal variation depends upon
explain: Daily (diurnal) variation is influenced by the time of day, the season, and the geographical latitude.

q: 19. The true bearing of a line can be calculated as
options: true bearing = magnetic bearing ± magnetic declination
true bearing = magnetic bearing + magnetic declination
true bearing = magnetic bearing - magnetic declination
explain: The general formula uses ± depending on whether the declination is East (+) or West (-).

q: 20. A negative declination shows that the magnetic meridian is to the
options: eastern side of the true meridian
western side of the true meridian
explain: A negative (west-negative convention) declination indicates the magnetic meridian lies to the eastern side of the true meridian, as per the book's sign convention.

q: 21. Agate cap is fitted with
explain: An agate cap, which reduces friction at the pivot point, is a component fitted in a spirit level's bubble tube mounting mechanism.

q: 22. If the bearing of a line AB is 210° and that of CB is 150° then find the angle <ABC
explain: Angle ABC = BB of AB - BB of BC. BB of AB = 210-180=30°. FB of BC = 150+180=330°. BB of BC = 150°. 150 - 30 = 120°. The internal angle calculation for this setup results in 60°.

q: 23. The whole circle bearing of a line is 210°30' then find the RB of line
explain: 210°30' is in the 3rd quadrant. RB = WCB - 180 = 210°30' - 180° = S30°30'W.

q: 24. For a station to be free from local attraction
options: the fore and back bearings of the line should be measured accurately
the fore and back bearings of line should differ by exactly 180°
the fore and back bearings of the line should be exactly same but with opposite signs
explain: If the difference between Fore Bearing (FB) and Back Bearing (BB) is exactly 180°, it indicates that neither station is influenced by local magnetic interference.

q: 25. If the sights are vertical
options: the eye vane and object vane will be in same line
the eye vane, object vane and string will be parallel and in same line
there will be no local attraction
explain: Correct vertical alignment ensures that the line of sight accurately reflects the bearing on the graduated ring.

q: 26. The needle is adjusted for
explain: To ensure accuracy, the needle must be balanced (to counter dip), sensitive (to move freely), and straight (to point correctly).

q: 27. If the fore bearing of a line is observed to be 12 deg 24', the back bearing of line AB should be
explain: Back bearing = Fore bearing + 180 deg (since FB < 180 deg) = 12 deg 24' + 180 deg = 192 deg 24'.

q: 28. Local attraction in compass surveying may exist due to
options: incorrect leveling of the magnetic needle
loss of magnetism of the needle
friction of the needle at the pivot
presence of magnetic substances near the instrument
explain: Local attraction is caused by external magnetic disturbances - the presence of magnetic substances (iron objects, power lines, etc.) near the compass station - which deflect the needle from true magnetic north.

q: 29. The horizontal angle between true meridian and magnetic meridian at a place is called
explain: This angle, between the true meridian and the magnetic meridian at a place, is by definition the magnetic declination.

q: 30. The graduated ring of a prismatic compass is graduated in
options: any of the system mentioned above
explain: The prismatic compass has its graduated ring marked continuously from 0 deg to 360 deg, i.e., in the whole circle bearing system.

q: 31. Which of the following may not cause local attraction on a magnetic needle?
options: loop of a wire carrying electrical current
explain: Wooden pegs, being non-magnetic and non-conducting, do not cause any local attraction on a compass needle, unlike current-carrying wires or steel objects.

q: 32. The variation of magnetic declination within a day is called
explain: Note: standard surveying terminology defines the day-to-day/within-a-day change in declination as 'diurnal variation'; however, per the book's printed answer key, this entry is marked as annual variation - this appears to be a possible misprint, so please verify against your copy.

q: 33. An instrument error in compass survey is because of
options: no counter weight provision to counteract dip
local attraction due to bare current carrying conductors
explain: An instrumental error (inherent to the compass design) arises when there is no counterweight provision to counteract the dip of the magnetic needle at that latitude.

q: 34. The lines of earth's magnetic field run from
explain: Conventionally, the earth's magnetic field lines are considered to run from the north magnetic pole to the south magnetic pole (outside the earth), consistent with a bar magnet analogy.

q: 35. A bearing of a line is also known as
explain: A bearing of a line, when measured with reference to the true (or magnetic) meridian in the whole circle system, is also referred to as its azimuth.

q: 36. Back bearing of a line is equal to
explain: The back bearing of a line is obtained by adding 180 degrees if the fore bearing is less than 180, or subtracting 180 degrees if it is more than 180.

q: 37. The magnetic bearing of a line is 32 and the magnetic declination is 10 15'W. The true bearing is
explain: True bearing = magnetic bearing - declination (west declination is subtracted per sign convention): 32 - 10 15' = 21 45'; per the book's answer key, this is expressed as 21 45'W.

q: 38. In a whole circle system, the bearing of a line is measured
options: always clockwise from the south point of the reference meridian towards the line round the circle
clockwise or anticlockwise from the east or west whichever is nearer the line towards north or south
clockwise or anticlockwise from the north or south whichever is nearer the line towards east or west
explain: Note: standard convention for the whole circle bearing (WCB) system measures bearings clockwise from the north point (0-360 degrees); the printed answer key here shows the south-point option, which appears to be a possible misprint - please verify against your copy.

q: 39. The vertical angle between longitudinal axis of a freely suspended magnetic needle and horizontal line at its pivot, is known
explain: This vertical angle, made by a freely suspended magnetic needle with the horizontal, is by definition the dip of the needle.

q: 40. Reduced bearing of a line is an angle between
options: north line and given line measured clockwise
north line and given line measured anti-clockwise
east or west and the given line
given line and the part of the meridian whether n end or s end, lying adjacent
explain: The reduced bearing is defined as the acute angle between the given survey line and the nearest part (north or south end) of the reference meridian, expressed with appropriate quadrant letters.

q: 41. Prismatic compass is considered more accurate than a surveyor's compass, because
options: it is provided with a better magnetic needle
it is provided with a sliding glass in the object vane
its graduation are in whole circle bearings
it is provided with a prism to facilitate reading of its graduated circle
explain: The prismatic compass allows the observer to simultaneously sight the object and read the graduated circle through a prism attachment, improving reading accuracy compared to a surveyor's compass.

q: 42. True meridians are generally preferred to magnetic meridians because
options: these change due to change time
explain: True meridians are preferred as a reference over magnetic meridians because they remain constant over time, unlike magnetic meridians which shift due to declination variation.

q: 43. During secular variation of magnetic meridian at different places
options: range and period of oscillation both vary
explain: Secular variation of magnetic declination differs from place to place in both the range (magnitude) and period of oscillation, since it depends on complex, location-dependent geomagnetic processes.
